subject: Art & Geometry
title: Shapes, Geometry & Art
subtitle: Visual Symmetry & Geometry in Everyday Life
author: Distinguished Curators & Academic Press

pages.title: The World of 2D Shapes: Flat Geometry
bulletPoints: A 2D shape is completely flat; it has length and width, but zero depth or thickness.
Vertices and edges: Straight lines are called edges or sides; points where edges meet are called vertices (corners).
The four primary flat shapes: Circles, Squares, Triangles, and Rectangles.
Nature's shapes: Orange slices are circles, honeycomb cells are hexagons, and pine needles form sharp lines.

pages.title: The Circle: The Infinite Curve
bulletPoints: A circle is perfectly round with zero straight edges and zero corners.
Center point: Every single point on the outer curved boundary is the exact same distance from the center point.
Radius and diameter: The distance from center to edge is the radius; all the way across through the center is diameter.
Artistic circles: Draw coins, wheel spokes, dinner plates, the full moon, and ripples in a pond.

pages.title: The Square: Perfect Four-Sided Balance
bulletPoints: A square has 4 straight sides of exactly equal length and 4 square corners (right angles, 90°).
Symmetry: A square has 4 lines of symmetry: vertical, horizontal, and both diagonal mirror lines.
Everyday squares: Chessboard tiles, window panes, sticky notes, and square picture frames.
Drawing tip: Use a ruler to make sure all 4 sides measure the exact same number of centimeters.

pages.title: Triangles: Three Corners & Infinite Variety
bulletPoints: A triangle is any closed shape with exactly 3 straight sides and 3 vertices (angles).
Equilateral triangle: All 3 sides are equal length and all 3 angles are identical (60°).
Isosceles triangle: 2 sides are equal, like a tall pine tree or a slice of birthday cake.
Right-angled triangle: Contains one sharp square corner (90°), like a carpenter's set square.

pages.title: Rectangles: Two Long and Two Short
bulletPoints: A rectangle has 4 straight sides and 4 right-angle square corners.
Opposite sides are parallel and exactly equal in length (2 long sides and 2 short sides).
A square is actually a special rectangle where all four sides happen to be equal!
Architecture all around: Doors, books, smartphones, bricks, and chalkboard screens are rectangles.

pages.title: Pentagons & Hexagons: Nature's Polygons
bulletPoints: Pentagon: A polygon with 5 straight sides and 5 vertices (like a classic house outline or star center).
Hexagon: A polygon with 6 straight sides and 6 vertices.
The bee's secret: Honeybee hives build hexagonal wax cells because hexagons enclose maximum honey with minimum wax!
Snowflakes: Every natural ice crystal snowflake has 6-fold hexagonal symmetry.

pages.title: Ovals & Diamonds: Squashed Circles & Tilted Squares
bulletPoints: Oval (Ellipse): A smooth, curved shape with no corners that looks like a gently stretched circle or an egg.
Diamond (Rhombus): A quadrilateral where all 4 sides are equal length, but corners are slanted rather than square.
Kite shape: Two pairs of equal-length adjacent sides flying up in the windy sky.
Art practice: Draw an oval bird body and add triangular beak and diamond tail feathers!

pages.title: 3D Solid Shapes: Length, Width & Depth
bulletPoints: Unlike flat 2D drawings, 3D solids occupy physical space: you can hold them in your hands!
Faces: The flat or curved surfaces of a 3D solid.
Edges: The straight lines where two faces meet.
Vertices: The sharp corner points where three or more edges intersect.

pages.title: The Sphere: Perfectly Smooth in All Directions
bulletPoints: A sphere is a completely round 3D solid with 1 continuous curved surface, 0 flat faces, 0 edges, and 0 vertices.
Rolling champion: Spheres roll smoothly in any direction because every surface point is equidistant from the center.
Spheres in the cosmos: Planets, moons, bubbles, marbles, and basketballs are all natural spheres.
Shadow play: In bright sunlight, a 3D sphere casts a flat 2D circular shadow on the ground.

pages.title: The Cube: Six Identical Square Faces
bulletPoints: A cube has 6 flat square faces, 12 straight edges of equal length, and 8 sharp corner vertices.
Stacking blocks: Cubes stack neatly on top of each other without rolling away.
Rolling dice: A game die is a cube; opposing faces always add up to 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4).
Sugar cubes and ice blocks: Perfect geometric solids found right inside kitchen pantries.

pages.title: The Cylinder: The Rolling Can
bulletPoints: A cylinder has 2 flat circular faces (top and bottom) and 1 smooth curved surface connecting them.
It has 2 curved edges and 0 sharp vertices.
Dual action: A cylinder can slide on its flat circular base or roll along its curved surface.
Cylinders everywhere: Soup cans, tree trunks, drinking glasses, pencil bodies, and batteries.

pages.title: The Cone: The Party Hat and Ice Cream Treat
bulletPoints: A cone has 1 flat circular base, 1 curved surface tapering smoothly to 1 sharp point (apex).
It has 1 circular edge and 1 apex vertex.
Volcanoes and mountains: Tectonic eruptions create natural cone-shaped volcanic peaks.
Everyday cones: Orange traffic safety cones, waffle ice cream cones, and festive birthday party hats.

pages.title: Symmetry: The Magic Mirror Line
bulletPoints: A shape has reflectional symmetry if a line can divide it into two identical halves that mirror each other.
Butterfly wings: The left wing has the exact same spots and colors as the right wing.
Human body: Draw an imaginary vertical line down the face: one eye, ear, and nostril on each side.
Fold test: If you fold a paper shape along its symmetry line, both halves align with zero overlap!

pages.title: Tessellations: Tiling Without Any Gaps
bulletPoints: A tessellation is a pattern of repeating shapes that fit together seamlessly with no gaps and no overlaps.
Regular tessellations: Only equilateral triangles, squares, and regular hexagons can tile a flat plane by themselves.
M.C. Escher: The famous artist created mind-bending tessellations of flying birds and swimming fish.
Bathroom tile design: Notice how hexagonal or square tiles cover the entire floor without leaving holes.

pages.title: Tangram Puzzles: The Ancient Seven Pieces
bulletPoints: The Tangram is a 1,000-year-old Chinese dissection puzzle made from a single square cut into 7 pieces (tans).
The 7 pieces: 2 large triangles, 1 medium triangle, 2 small triangles, 1 square, and 1 parallelogram.
Creativity rule: Use all 7 pieces without overlapping to create silhouettes of animals, ships, and running people.
Spatial thinking: Discovering how two small triangles join together to form a square or a larger triangle.

pages.title: Geometric Modern Art: Mondrian and Kandinsky
bulletPoints: Piet Mondrian: Dutch painter famous for grid paintings using thick black lines and primary color squares (red, yellow, blue).
Wassily Kandinsky: Russian master who used concentric colorful circles, sharp triangles, and dynamic lines to express music.
Abstract art: Instead of painting realistic trees, artists use geometry to evoke emotions and harmony.
Try it yourself: Use black markers to draw intersecting lines, then fill geometric pockets with contrasting watercolors.

pages.title: Origami: The Japanese Art of Paper Folding
bulletPoints: Origami transforms a simple flat square sheet of colored paper into a 3D sculpture through folding alone.
No scissors or glue: Traditional origami relies purely on geometric valley folds, mountain folds, and symmetry.
The Peace Crane (Orizuru): Folding paper triangles repeatedly creates wings, neck, and tail of a graceful flying bird.
Geometry in action: Unfolding an origami crane reveals a complex, beautiful crease pattern of symmetric geometric tessellations.

pages.title: Shapes in Architecture: Arches, Domes & Pyramids
bulletPoints: Roman Arches: Semicircular arches distribute heavy stone weight outward and downward, creating strong bridges.
The Great Pyramids: Broad square bases tapering to a top apex make pyramids one of the most stable structures on Earth.
Geodesic Domes: Buckminster Fuller designed spherical domes made entirely of interlocking triangles for lightweight strength.
Skyline silhouettes: City skyscrapers combine rectangles, cylinders, and spires reaching into the clouds.

pages.title: Shadow Shapes: How 3D Objects Cast 2D Shadows
bulletPoints: When an opaque 3D object blocks rays of light, it casts a flat 2D shadow onto the surface behind it.
Cube shadows: Depending on angle, a cube can cast a square, rectangle, or even a 6-sided hexagonal shadow!
Cylinder shadows: Shining light from the top casts a circle; shining light from the side casts a rectangle.
Hand shadow puppetry: Shape your fingers into geometric profiles to cast barking dogs, flying geese, and hopping bunnies.

pages.title: The Grand Gallery Exhibition: Dream Geometric Castle
bulletPoints: Project challenge: Create your ultimate fantasy castle using at least 5 different 2D and 3D geometric shapes.
Tower cylinders topped with sharp cone roofs; square brick walls pierced with rectangular archway gates.
Triangular flags fluttering from towers; circular stained glass windows glowing with rainbow colors.
Celebrate your artwork: Sign your name in the corner of your masterpiece—you are a true Shape and Geometry Artist!
